newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - October looking firm.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - October looking firm.

text.p: Gulf oil product prices have further upside potential as long as U.S. and European markets are seized by winter stockbuilding, Gulf oil traders said on Thursday.
A four-month-long surge has pushed gas oil to its highest level since the 1991 Gulf War even before an anticipated rise in demand as firms lock in late 1996/early 1997 supplies.
"October barrels are nearly gone, November is also seeing good demand," a product trader based in the region said.
Gas oil was quoted at $28.20 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, its strongest level since February 1991 during the height of the Gulf War which ended Iraq's occupation of Kuwait.
Supplies of 0.5 percent sulphur gas oil in the Gulf were tight with supplies for October said to be already sold out, the last Kuwaiti cargo being sold to a trader this week.
A wide Gulf-Mediterranean differential has also encouraged traders to place Gulf gas oil into east Africa, traders said.
Cargoes were offered at a 90 cents to $1.05 premium.
The bullish impact of low inventories in key consumer markets has also been felt across the Gulf barrel with kerosene, naphtha and 380 cst grade fuel oil prices hugging year highs.

Kerosene fundamentals were far less bullish than gas oil because of muted Japanese demand, though in the short term the market will be set by Indian Oil Corp's (IOC) November tender which is expected to be awarded on Friday, traders said.
Gulf traders said an award of more than three or four cargoes would support the market.
The apparent withdrawl of Japanese buying has left late October cargoes available, and one cargo was said by traders to have been traded at only a 5-10 cent premium to quotes.
Middle distillate markets will also take their cue from IOC's term negotiations with Gulf refiners which would give an indication to IOC's spot market requirements.
"India has become the biggest factor and outlet for middle distillates in the crude," a trader at a state refiner said.
"Even additional term volumes may not cover the demand is India which is continually growing," another trader said.
IOC has already tied up term supplies with Kuwait, and Abu Dhabi is in negotiations with Saudi Arabia for middle distillates and will begin talks with Bahrain next week.
For leading state refiners in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, the price rally coincides with 1997 term contract negotiations with international firms.
Companies wanting to lift naphtha from Saudi Aramco have till October 4 to submit initial volume and price indications for 1997 deliveries from Ras Tanura, Jubail and Rabigh.
Traders said they expect Aramco to press for at least a 50-cent increase in Gulf and Red Sea premiums for 1997 naphtha.
Aramco is studying buyers' proposals for term deliveries of gas oil, kerosene and fuel oil.
-- Steven Swindells, Dubai Newsroom, +971 4 6071255
